column2: Then Bhima, taking his mace with its great tip and wearing armour, bore a form, great king, like Garuda's.
With helmet bound and wearing golden armour in the battle, your son shone, O king, like a golden king of mountains.
Both heroes, Bhima and Duryodhana, clad in armour, shone in the fight like two enraged elephants.
Standing in the middle of the arena, those two brothers, bulls among men, shone, great king, like the risen moon and sun.
They looked at one another like two angry great elephants, burning each other with their eyes, O king, each wishing to slay the other.
With a delighted mind, O king, the Kaurava took his mace, licking the corners of his mouth, his eyes red with anger, panting.
Then King Duryodhana, valiant, taking his mace, looked at Bhimasena and challenged him as an elephant challenges an elephant.
Bhima, valiant, taking up his mace of iron likewise, challenged the king as a lion challenges a lion in the forest.
Those two, Duryodhana and Vrikodara, with maces raised in their hands, shone in the fight like two mountains with peaks.
Both were enraged, both of terrible valour, both pupils in mace-fighting of the wise son of Rohini.
Both of similar deeds, like Yama and Vasava, likewise of similar deeds were the two mighty ones, like Varuna,
like Vasudeva and Rama, and like Vaishravana, great king; they were like Madhu and Kaitabha in battle.
Both of like deeds in the fight, like Sunda and Upasunda, scorchers of foes, equal to Time and Death.
Rushing at one another like two rutting great elephants in a contest over a cow-elephant, proud, fierce with rut as in autumn,
like two furious elephants eager to conquer, bulls of the Bharatas, both spewing blazing venom of anger like serpents.
Both enraged at each other, looking on each other, subduers of foes, both tigers of the Bharatas, endowed with prowess,
hard to assail like two lions in the mace-fight, scorchers of foes, with nails and fangs as weapons, hard to bear like two tigers,
troubled like two oceans at the dissolution of creatures, hard to cross, enraged like two red planets, blazing great chariot-warriors,
radiant great souls, mighty and shining, the two best of the Kurus appeared like Time and the risen sun.
Greatly enraged like two tigers, like two roaring clouds, the two mighty-armed ones rejoiced like two maned lions.
Greatly enraged like two elephants, like two blazing fires, those two great souls were seen like two mountains with peaks.
Their lips trembling with anger, looking at each other, those two great souls, best of men, came together, maces in hand.
Both greatly delighted, both highly esteemed, neighing like two fine horses, trumpeting like two elephants,
roaring like two bulls, Duryodhana and Vrikodara, mad with strength like two Daityas, shone, those two best of men.
Then, O king, Duryodhana said this to Yudhishthira, who stood with the Srinjayas, blazing like the sun:
This battle has been resolved between me and Bhima; sit down and watch the clash, best of kings.
Then that vast circle of kings sat down, shining like the circle of the sun in the sky.
In their midst the mighty-armed and glorious elder brother of Keshava sat, honoured on every side.
In the midst of the kings, clad in blue and white-lustred, he shone like the moon at night, full and surrounded by stars.
Those two, great king, mace in hand, hard to approach, stood hewing at one another with fierce words.
Having then said unpleasant things to each other, those two bulls of the Kurus stood looking at one another like Vritra and Shakra in battle.

Fie on human life, whose end is such, where my son, master of eleven divisions,
mahabharata:9:55.3	having commanded all the kings and enjoyed this earth, goes to battle on foot, famed, with a mace in hand, swiftly.
mahabharata:9:55.4	Having been lord of the world, my son, as if lordless, goes with mace raised; what is this but fate?
mahabharata:9:55.5	Ah, great sorrow has come to me through my son, Sanjaya. Having said this, the lord of men, afflicted with grief, fell silent.
[Sanjaya said:] With a voice like thunder, bellowing with joy like a bull, the valiant one then challenged Partha to battle.
When the king of the Kurus, the great soul, challenged Bhima, very dreadful portents of many kinds appeared.
Winds blew with thunder-crashes, dust rained down, and all the quarters were covered with darkness.
Great-sounding thunderbolts, tumultuous and hair-raising, fell, and meteors by the hundred burst across the sky.
Rahu swallowed the sun out of season, lord of men, and the earth with its forests and trees shook with a great quake.
Rough winds blew low, raining gravel, and peaks of mountains fell to the ground.
Beasts of many shapes ran in the ten directions, and blazing jackals howled, dreadful and very terrible.
Dreadful, hair-raising thunderclaps came in the blazing quarter, O king of kings, and beasts spoke ill omens.
The waters in wells rose on every side, and bodiless great cries were heard then, O king.
Seeing these and other portents, Vrikodara said to his elder brother Yudhishthira, king of dharma:

This dull-souled Suyodhana cannot conquer me in battle. Today I shall release the anger long hidden in my heart upon Suyodhana, king of the Kauravas, as Fire released it upon Khandava.
mahabharata:9:55.17	Today I shall pull out the dart in your heart, Pandava, slaying with my mace this sinner, the vilest of the Kuru family.
mahabharata:9:55.18	Today I shall place on you the garland of fame, having slain this evildoer with my mace at the head of the battle.
mahabharata:9:55.19	Today I shall break his body into a hundred pieces with this mace; he shall not again enter the city called Varanasahvaya (Hastinapura).
mahabharata:9:55.20	For setting serpents on my bed, poison in my food, the fall at Pramanakoti, the burning in the house of lac,
mahabharata:9:55.21	the derision in the assembly, the seizing of all we had, the year of living unknown and the dwelling in the forest, blameless one,
mahabharata:9:55.22	today I shall reach the end of these sorrows, best of the Bharatas; having slain him in a single day I shall be free of my debt.
Today the life of the ill-minded, unrefined son of Dhritarashtra, best of the Bharatas, comes to an end, and his seeing his mother and father.
Today this defiler of the line of Shantanu, king of the Kurus, shall lie on the ground, having given up life, fortune and kingdom.
And King Dhritarashtra today, hearing his son slain by me, will remember the evil deed born of Shakuni's counsel."
Having said this, tiger among kings, the valiant one took his mace and stood for battle, challenging as Shakra challenged Vritra.
Seeing him with mace raised, like Kailasa with its peaks, Bhimasena again, enraged, spoke to Duryodhana:

Remember that evil deed of King Dhritarashtra and of yourself, what happened at Varanavata,
mahabharata:9:55.29	and Draupadi tormented in the assembly in her season, and the king (Yudhishthira) cheated at dice by you and the son of Subala,
mahabharata:9:55.30	and the great suffering we endured in the forest because of you, and in the city of Virata as if in another womb—I shall repay all that today; by good fortune I see you, ill-minded one.
mahabharata:9:55.31	Because of you the mighty son of Ganga, best of chariot-warriors, lies on a bed of arrows, slain by the son of Yajnasena (Shikhandin).
mahabharata:9:55.32	Drona is slain, and Karna, and the mighty Shalya, and Shakuni son of Subala, the first author of the enmity, is slain.
mahabharata:9:55.33	The sinful Pratikamin who tormented Draupadi is slain, and all your brothers are slain, heroes of valorous fighting.
mahabharata:9:55.34	These and many other kings have been slain because of you; today I shall slay you with my mace, without doubt.
To Vrikodara, speaking thus loudly, O king of kings, your son, fearless and truly valiant, replied:

Why boast so much? Fight, Vrikodara. Today I shall remove your eagerness for battle, vilest of your family.
mahabharata:9:55.37	Duryodhana cannot be frightened by words by anyone like you, as an ordinary man might be.
mahabharata:9:55.38	By good fortune this mace-fight with you, long desired and lodged in my heart, has been brought about by the gods.
mahabharata:9:55.39	What use is speech, ill-minded one, or much boasting? Let this speech become deed; do not delay.
Hearing his words, all the kings and the Somakas who were assembled there applauded.
Then, honoured by all, his hair standing on end with joy, the delight of the Kurus again steadied his mind for battle.
The kings again cheered the intolerant Duryodhana, like a rutting elephant, by clapping their hands.
Then the great-souled Pandava Vrikodara, raising his mace, rushed swiftly at the great-souled son of Dhritarashtra.
Elephants trumpeted there and horses neighed repeatedly, and the weapons of the victory-seeking Pandavas blazed.
The two, bellowing, closed in like two horned bulls, and a great thunderous sound came from their encounter.
There was a tumultuous, hair-raising fight between the two, each eager to win in battle, like Indra and Prahlada.
With all their limbs drenched in blood, mace in hand, spirited and great-souled, they looked like two flowering kimshuka trees.
As that dreadful great battle went on, the sky, as though with swarms of fireflies, shone, beautiful to behold.
As that crowded, tumultuous fight went on, both became exhausted as they fought, subduers of foes.
After resting a moment, those scorchers of foes again attacked, raising their fine maces.
Seeing them refreshed, those two mighty bulls among men, like two strong rutting elephants in a contest over a cow-elephant,
seeing both of boundless prowess with maces raised, the gods, Gandharvas and Danavas fell into supreme wonder.
Seeing Duryodhana and Vrikodara with maces raised, doubt about the victory arose in all beings.
Coming together again, those two brothers, best of the strong, each seeking an opening in the other, watched for the chance.
The spectators, O king, saw the heavy, dreadful, flesh-rending mace, like Yama's rod, raised like Indra's thunderbolt.
As Bhimasena whirled his mace in the battle, a very tumultuous and dreadful sound arose for a moment.
Seeing the Pandava whirling it, Dhritarashtra's son was astonished at the heavy mace of swift speed.
Moving in various paths and circles, Bharata, the hero Vrikodara then shone again.
Meeting each other, guarding against each other, they struck again and again, like two cats over food.
Bhimasena moved in many kinds of paths, in wondrous circles and various stances,
in cow's-urine curves and wondrous advances and retreats, in avoiding and dodging blows, in running around,
in rushing in, thrusting, standing fast in conflict, turning, whirling, leaping and bounding, in feints and counter-feints, both skilled in mace-fighting.
Thus moving, the two best of the Kurus struck at each other, and deceiving each other roamed again.
Sporting, very strong, they moved in circles, and mace in hand, those two mighty ones stood in their circles.
Dhritarashtra's son moved to the right circle, O king, and Bhimasena moved to the left circle.
As Bhima moved thus at the head of the battle, Duryodhana, great king, struck him on the side.
Struck then by your son, Bharata, Bhima whirled his heavy mace, heedless of the blow.
They saw, great king, Bhimasena's dreadful mace, like Indra's thunderbolt, raised like Yama's rod.
Seeing Bhimasena whirling his mace, your son, subduer of foes, raised his dreadful mace and struck back.
From the mace of your son, with the speed of the wind, Bharata, a tumultuous sound arose and fire sprang forth.
Moving in various paths and circles by parts, the splendid Suyodhana shone more than Bhima.
The great mace whirled by Bhima with all his speed emitted fire with smoke and flame, fierce and loud.
Seeing the mace whirled by Bhimasena, Suyodhana whirled his heavy mace of iron and shone greatly.
Seeing the wind-speed of that great soul's mace, fear entered all the Pandavas with the Somakas.
Displaying everywhere the sport of battle in the fight, those two subduers of foes suddenly struck each other with their maces.
Meeting, they shone, great king, like two elephants with tusks, drenched in blood.
Thus that battle was dreadful and unconcealed, cruel as the day turned, like that of Vritra and Vasava.
Seeing Bhima standing, your mighty son, moving in the most wondrous paths, rushed at the son of Kunti.
His heavy, gold-adorned mace, as he was enraged, the enraged Bhima struck.
A noise with sparks from the collision of the two arose, great king, like that of two thunderbolts released.
As that swift mace hurled by Bhimasena fell, the earth shook, great king.
The Kaurava could not bear that mace repelled in the battle, like a rutting elephant enraged at the sight of a rival elephant.
He, having resolved, circled to the left, O king, and struck the son of Kunti on the head with his terrible-speed mace.
Though struck by that mace of your son, Pandava Bhima did not tremble, great king, and it was wondrous.
And that was a marvel, O king, that all the armies praised: that Bhima, struck by the mace, did not move a step.
Then Bhima of terrible valour hurled at Duryodhana a heavier, blazing mace adorned with gold.
Undisturbed, the mighty one made that blow vain by his agility, and there was great astonishment.
That vain mace, falling, driven by Bhima, shook the earth with a great thunderous sound.
Taking the Kaushika paths and leaping again and again, understanding the fall of the mace, he evaded Bhimasena.
Having thus eluded Bhima, the best of the Kurus, enraged and mighty, struck him with the mace on the chest.
Struck by the mace, Bhima, faint in the great battle, did not know what to do, being struck by your son.
As that went on, O king, the Somakas and Pandavas, their resolve greatly shaken, lost their gladness of mind.
But he, enraged by that blow like an elephant, rushed at your son like elephant at elephant.
Then Bhima, impetuous, rushed with his mace at your son, with speed, like a lion at a forest elephant.
Approaching the king, skilled in releasing the mace, he whirled his mace, O king, aiming at your son.
Bhimasena then struck Duryodhana on the side; stunned by the blow, he fell to his knees on the ground.
When that best of the Bharatas had gone to his knees on the earth, a cry arose from the Srinjayas, lord of the world.
Hearing the cry of the Srinjayas, your son, best of men, grew angry in indignation, best of the Bharatas.
The mighty-armed one rose, enraged, hissing like a serpent, and looked at Bhimasena as if to burn him with his eyes.
Then that best of the Bharatas, mace in hand, rushed as if to crush Bhimasena's head in the battle.
That great soul of terrible valour struck the great-souled Bhima on the temple, and he stood firm like a mountain.
Pritha's son, struck by the mace in the battle, shone the more, O king, with blood gushing out, like an elephant with rut streaming.
Then, taking up his iron mace, deadly, with a sound like thunderbolt, the elder brother of Dhananjaya, tormentor of foes, valiantly struck his enemy with force.
Struck by Bhimasena, your son fell, his bodily frame shaken, like a flowering sala tree struck by the wind and whirled in a great forest.
Then the Pandavas roared and rejoiced, seeing your son fallen on the ground; and your son, regaining consciousness, leapt up like an elephant from a lake.
That king, ever intolerant, a great chariot-warrior, circling as one trained, struck the Pandava standing before him, who, with limbs shaken, touched the ground.
The Kaurava roared loud, having felled Bhima to the ground in the fight with force, and with a mace-blow of thunderbolt-like splendour broke Bhima's protective armour.
Then a great sound arose in the sky from the dwellers in heaven and the Apsarases, who shouted, and a most excellent rain of wondrous flowers fell, hurled by them.
Then supreme fear entered the Pandavas, seeing the best of men fallen to the ground and the Kaurava undiminished in strength, and hearing of the breaking of the firm armour.
Then after a moment, regaining consciousness, wiping his face half-covered with blood, Vrikodara steadied himself, his eyes rolling, and stood firm with force.
Of these two heroes in the fight, which, in your view, is likely to win, Janardana? Or whose merit is the greater? Tell me this.
[Vasudeva said:] "The teaching of the two is equal; Bhima is the stronger, but Dhritarashtra's son has trained harder than Vrikodara.
Bhimasena, fighting by dharma, will not win; but fighting unfairly he may slay this Suyodhana.

We have heard that the asuras were conquered by the gods through illusion, and that Virochana was conquered by Shakra through illusion, friend; and by illusion the slayer of Bala snatched away Vritra's energy.
Bhima made a vow at the time of the dice-game, Dhananjaya: 'I shall break your thighs in battle with my mace, Suyodhana.'
Let that scorcher of foes fulfil that vow too, and let him cut down by illusion the illusionist king.
If he fights fairly, relying on strength, Yudhishthira will fall into difficulty.
I shall say again, Pandava; hear it from me. Through the fault of the king of dharma fear has come upon us again.
This is a great folly of the king of dharma, Pandava, that he staked such a wager on a single victory in the fight: Suyodhana is skilled and a hero, and he has nowhere to flee.
An ancient verse sung by Ushanas is also heard, full of true meaning; hear it as I recite it.
'For those who return, broken, desiring life, the remnants of an enemy must be feared; for they are on a single path.'
This Suyodhana is broken, his army slain, gone into the lake, defeated, wishing for the forest, hopeless of regaining the kingdom.
What wise man would challenge him again to a duel on equal terms? Would Suyodhana not take back the kingdom you won?
He who for thirteen years trained with the mace, moving up and down and across, wishing to slay Bhimasena,
if the mighty-armed one does not slay him unfairly, this Kaurava, Dhritarashtra's son, will be your king."
Hearing this from the great-souled Keshava, Dhananjaya struck his thigh with his hand in sight of Bhimasena.
Taking the signal, Bhima moved in the battle with his mace in wondrous circles, paired and unpaired.
The Pandava moved to the right circle, the left, and the cow's-urine curve, O king, as if bewildering his foe.
Likewise your son, skilled in the paths of the mace, moved lightly and wondrously, wishing to slay Bhimasena.
Whirling their dreadful maces, smeared with sandal and aloe, wishing to end the enmity, they were like two Deaths enraged in the battle.
Each wishing to slay the other, those two heroes, bulls among men, fought like two Garudas eager for a serpent.
As those two Bhimas moved in wondrous circles, O king, sparks of fire sprang from the collision of their maces.
As those two heroes, strong in battle, struck equally, they were like two oceans lashed by the wind, O king.
As they struck equally, like two rutting elephants, the thunderous sound of the mace-blows arose.
In that dreadful and crowded encounter, both became exhausted as they fought, subduers of foes.
After resting a moment, those two scorchers of foes, enraged, again attacked, raising their great maces.
Between them a dreadful and unconcealed battle took place with falls of maces, O king of kings, as they hewed at one another.
Driven by exertion, bull-eyed and strong, the two heroes struck each other like two buffaloes standing in mud.
With all their limbs battered and drenched in blood, they looked like two flowering kimshuka trees on the Himalaya.
When Duryodhana showed an opening, the Pandava, smiling slightly, suddenly rose to the attack.
Seeing the stratagem the owl had worked in the night, Drona's son alone, with a resolve formed on that model, reflected.
All were students of the Veda, all had completed their vows, all were facing the enemy and fell—what is there to lament?
How did the earth swallow his chariot-wheel in battle, and how was my brother cursed? You ought to tell me this.
[The serpent said:] "As greedy priests offering oblations in a sacrifice gain no fruit here or in the next world, so too is it with me."
By austerities, sacrifices and giving, Yudhishthira, men who do sin cross over it always.
And always rising at dawn, after reciting his prayers, pure, the king prayed for the Pandavas' unconquered success in battles.
Seeing thus that the turn of Time had come, Hrishikesha, on the thirteenth day of the new moon, seeing those portents, said this:
Turning back to the north, those best of the Bharatas, followers of yoga, went, wishing to circumambulate the earth.
Strewn with bones and hair, swarming with worms and insects, surrounded all round by blazing fire.
